common_name: Yellow Jersey Sweet Potato (Dry-Fleshed Southern Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant rooted slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil is thoroughly warm, in loose, well-drained soil built into ridges in full sun; Yellow Jersey is an old Southern heirloom grown for its pale yellow skin and dry, mealy flesh, a different texture than modern moist orange types like Beauregard.

directions: Plant rooted slips 4-6 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil formed into ridges in full sun. Yellow Jersey is an old-fashioned Southern heirloom with pale yellow-tan skin and light yellow, dry, mealy flesh, a texture closer to a baking potato than the moist, syrupy sweetness of modern orange-fleshed varieties, and it was once among the most widely grown sweet potatoes in the South before moister types like Beauregard became dominant. Vines are moderately vigorous and productive, and the drier flesh makes the roots well suited to baking and frying rather than the candied dishes moist types are typically used for. Dig once vines begin to yellow in fall and before the first frost, and cure the roots at warm temperatures and high humidity for a week or two to heal cuts, firm the skin, and develop full sweetness before storing.

common_name: Cordner Sweet Potato (Louisiana Heirloom Baking Sweet Potato)

planting.note: Plant rooted slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil is thoroughly warm, in loose, well-drained soil built into ridges in full sun; Cordner is a Louisiana heirloom sweet potato with purple-blushed skin and moist orange flesh, long grown by home gardeners in the Gulf South.

directions: Plant rooted slips 4-6 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil formed into ridges in full sun, and hill soil up over the row as vines run to keep developing roots covered. Cordner is a Louisiana dooryard heirloom with pinkish-purple-blushed skin and moist, deep-orange flesh that bakes up sweet and soft, grown by Gulf South home gardeners for generations before modern commercial varieties took over most production. The vigorous, sprawling vines tolerate the heat and humidity of a Louisiana summer with ease and provide good ground cover that shades out weeds once established. Dig roots once vines begin to yellow in fall and before frost threatens, and cure at warm temperatures and high humidity for one to two weeks to firm the skin and sweeten the flesh before storing in a cool, dry place.

common_name: Curly Locks Hosta (Wavy Gold-Centered Narrow-Leaf Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Curly Locks is a sport of Praying Hands with the same narrow, upright leaf form but with wavy, twisted margins and a bright gold leaf center.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, with a little morning sun to bring out the brightest gold coloring in the leaf centers. Curly Locks arose as a sport of the narrow-leaf novelty hosta Praying Hands and keeps its parent's distinctive upright, folded leaf form while adding wavy, twisted margins and a strong gold center against dark green edges, giving the clump an even more sculptural, textural look. The narrow, vertical habit makes it stand out sharply against broad-leaved hosta neighbors and works well as a specimen in a container or at the front of a shaded border. Pale lavender flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer. Divide congested clumps in spring every three to four years and watch for slugs on the tender emerging growth.

common_name: Dolce Licorice Heuchera (Near-Black Foliage Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Dolce Licorice is part of the Proven Winners Dolce series, grown for its near-black, glossy foliage that holds its dark color through the season better than many purple heucheras.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, with protection from hot afternoon sun in the Gulf South to keep the foliage from bleaching. Dolce Licorice is part of the Proven Winners Dolce breeding series, selected for deep, glossy, near-black leaves with a ruffled edge that hold their dramatic color from spring through fall rather than fading to green in summer heat the way many dark-leaved heucheras do. Airy sprays of small white flowers rise above the foliage on wiry stems in early summer and draw in pollinators, though the foliage remains the main attraction. Its compact size suits container plantings, mixed shade borders, and edging, where the dark color makes a strong contrast against silver or chartreuse companions. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring, resetting the crown at its original depth.
